translation_direction: fr → vi; direct from the specifically identified complete French electronic witness
ai_disclosure: Direct AI-produced Vietnamese prose by Claude Opus 5.5. The drafting system conducted the final full assessment; a separate-context assessment by the same model family read every pair and supplied findings first. No human translator, editor, reviewer, independent model consensus or actual reader feedback is recorded.

entry_conditions: Complete named-source and Vietnamese texts, explicit alignment and exact content hashes.
Compare every source and target passage; disclose that this assessor also revised the text and has seen earlier AI assessments.
Source and target edition titles are present and compared explicitly; the title review must match both catalog title strings exactly.
exit_conditions: One complete AI review with a weighted score at least 8.6 using the five unchanged weights and half-point category scores; no separate numerical dimension floors.
All canonical passages reviewed; no unresolved major or critical finding; source and target hashes match the final text.
Publication and rights status are recorded separately in the edition catalog; an AI score does not supply a license.
The selected review includes source_title, target_title and a substantive title rationale; changed titles require a fresh matching review.
review_process.human_feedback: Optional after publication or while a work remains a draft; no prior human publication review is required by v2.

decisions.decision: Molière’s prose is kept as brisk, speakable Vietnamese with each character’s register distinct: Harpagon’s stinginess and rage, Frosine’s flattery, Maître Jacques’s two hats, the lovers’ graceful anh/em.
decisions.rationale: The comedy is in the differentiated voices.

decisions.decision: The French text comes from French Wikisource’s Louandre edition; the editor’s Notice and footnotes were removed; the source’s scene-numbering irregularities are kept.

revision_history.scope: Complete initial direct translation, separate-context full source/target assessment and concrete revisions before the selected final review.

changes.explanation: Harpagon calls his son Cléante ‘tao/mày’ in the quarrel, against the glossary’s fixed ‘cha/con’. The French has the rude ‘tu’ there, so the glossary was amended after the review to allow the rage register in these scenes; no text change.
Harpagon calls Maître Jacques ‘tao/mày’ in the interrogation against the fixed ‘tôi/anh’. Again the French is the rude ‘tu’; the glossary was amended to allow it, no text change.
‘Fable’ (a byword) was rendered as ‘chuyện bịa’; now ‘đề tài đàm tiếu’.
‘En de trop belles mains’ was a comparative; now hands too fair to give it back.
The garbled ‘quỷ thật là’ now ‘cái khó chết tiệt là’.
An ambiguous ‘cậu’ in Jacques’s report now ‘cậu ấy’.
The unfinished ‘Cha là người mẹ con đã khóc’ was completed.
The garbled ‘xin em từ ông’ was corrected.

selection_limit: Chosen for a complete, directly sourced and openly reusable Vietnamese edition. Existing Vietnamese translations, their quality and reader demand have not been comprehensively assessed; no absence or superiority claim is made.

glossary.rationale: One rendering for the strongbox; big/small is kept only for Jacques’s gag.

glossary.source_term: Il faut manger pour vivre, et non pas vivre pour manger.
glossary.draft_rendering: Phải ăn để sống, chứ không phải sống để ăn.
cha/con with his children; tao/mày with servants and, in rage, with Cléante and Jacques; tôi/anh with Maître Jacques when calm
glossary.rationale: Register is his character; the rage shift mirrors the French ‘tu’.

witness_decision: Selected the French Wikisource transcription of L’Avare from Charles Louandre’s edition (Œuvres complètes de Molière, Charpentier, 1910, vol. III); the project did not collate it with the 1669 first edition.

unresolved_questions.explanation: Harpagon’s ‘Rồi anh xem’ to the commissaire (976) still uses ‘anh’ where ‘ông’ would follow the address rule.
Harpagon’s self-reference moves between ‘ta’, ‘tao’ and ‘cha’ in the last confrontation.
‘Lunettes’ is ‘kính’ throughout, so the spectacles/telescope joke is clear only by context.

title_review.rationale: The title is rendered as ‘Lão hà tiện’ (The Old Miser); no earlier Vietnamese title was checked.

passage_assessment_notes.assessment: The opening of Act I: Valère and Élise.
The last unit, closing Act V.
